claim: Ticagrelor reduces cardiovascular events compared with clopidogrel in acute coronary syndromes
gold_rationale: Clinical and regulatory consensus supports the claim. The pivotal PLATO trial (Wallentin, NEJM 2009; n=18,624 ACS with/without ST-elevation) met its primary endpoint — the MACE composite of vascular death, MI, or stroke fell from 11.7% with clopidogrel to 9.8% with ticagrelor (HR 0.84, 95% CI 0.77-0.92, P<0.001), with a mortality reduction and no increase in overall major bleeding. On this evidence the FDA approved ticagrelor (BRILINTA) in 2011 to reduce thrombotic cardiovascular events in ACS, and ACC/AHA and ESC guidelines give ticagrelor a preferred (over clopidogrel) recommendation in ACS. The claim is therefore Supported as the mainstream consensus. Two caveats keep it from being 'dramatic'/all-or-none: (1) East Asian dedicated trials — PHILO (Goto, Circ J 2015; n=801) and TICAKOREA (Park, Circulation 2019; n=800) — did not reproduce PLATO's efficacy signal and showed numerically or significantly more bleeding, so a population-specific attenuation exists; and (2) ticagrelor's superiority is over clopidogrel specifically, not over prasugrel (ISAR-REACT 5 favored prasugrel, but that is a different comparator and outside this claim). Net: robust, guideline-endorsed support for the ticagrelor-vs-clopidogrel MACE-reduction claim in the general ACS population.
outcome: MACE composite (cardiovascular/vascular death, myocardial infarction, stroke)
population: Acute coronary syndromes (STEMI and NSTE-ACS), managed medically or invasively

baseline.text: Yes. Ticagrelor reduces cardiovascular events compared with clopidogrel in acute coronary syndromes. This is established by the landmark PLATO trial (NEJM 2009), a double-blind RCT of 18,624 ACS patients, in which the primary MACE composite (vascular death, MI, or stroke) occurred in 9.8% of ticagrelor patients vs 11.7% of clopidogrel patients (HR 0.84, 95% CI 0.77-0.92, P<0.001), including a reduction in cardiovascular and all-cause mortality, without an increase in overall major bleeding (though more non-CABG-related bleeding). On this basis the FDA approved ticagrelor for ACS in 2011 and major guidelines (ACC/AHA, ESC) recommend it preferentially over clopidogrel. The main nuances: East Asian populations (PHILO, TICAKOREA) did not replicate the efficacy benefit and showed more bleeding, and ticagrelor did not beat prasugrel in ISAR-REACT 5 — but versus clopidogrel specifically, the cardiovascular-event reduction is well supported.

rows.citation: Wallentin L, et al. Ticagrelor versus clopidogrel in patients with acute coronary syndromes (PLATO). N Engl J Med. 2009;361(11):1045-1057. DOI:10.1056/NEJMoa0904327. NCT00391872.
rows.integrity_note: Landmark double-blind pivotal RCT; regional heterogeneity (US sites) later scrutinized but result upheld by regulators. Title/design/N/effect re-verified exactly against PubMed abstract.
rows.finding: Primary MACE composite (vascular death, MI, stroke) 9.8% ticagrelor vs 11.7% clopidogrel at 12 mo (HR 0.84, 95% CI 0.77-0.92, P<0.001); CV and all-cause mortality also reduced (any-cause death 4.5% vs 5.9%, P<0.001); no increase in overall major bleeding (11.6% vs 11.2%, P=0.43) but more non-CABG bleeding (4.5% vs 3.8%, P=0.03).

rows.citation: A Comparison of Ticagrelor (AZD6140) and Clopidogrel in Patients With Acute Coronary Syndrome (PLATO). ClinicalTrials.gov NCT00391872 (COMPLETED; Phase 3; n=18,624).
rows.integrity_note: Registry record re-verified: COMPLETED, Phase 3, n=18,624, condition Acute Coronary Syndrome, interventions Ticagrelor vs Clopidogrel — matches the pivotal publication.
rows.finding: Registered pivotal Phase 3 ACS trial, ticagrelor vs clopidogrel, primary composite of CV death/MI/stroke; basis for FDA approval and guideline recommendations.

rows.citation: Goto S, et al. Ticagrelor vs. clopidogrel in Japanese, Korean and Taiwanese patients with ACS — phase III PHILO study. Circ J. 2015;79(11):2452-2460. DOI:10.1253/circj.CJ-15-0112.
rows.integrity_note: Underpowered East Asian dedicated RCT; authors attribute null result to small sample and few events. Numbers re-verified against PubMed abstract.
rows.finding: East Asian ACS (n=801): composite efficacy endpoint (MI/stroke/vascular death) 9.0% ticagrelor vs 6.3% clopidogrel (HR 1.47, 95% CI 0.88-2.44, NS); major bleeding numerically higher with ticagrelor (10.3% vs 6.8%, HR 1.54, 95% CI 0.94-2.53, NS) — did not reproduce PLATO benefit.

rows.citation: Park DW, et al. Clinically Significant Bleeding With Ticagrelor Versus Clopidogrel in Korean Patients With ACS Intended for Invasive Management (TICAKOREA): A Randomized Clinical Trial. Circulation. 2019;140(23):1865-1877. DOI:10.1161/CIRCULATIONAHA.119.041766. NCT02094963.
rows.integrity_note: Primary endpoint was a bleeding SAFETY outcome (clinically significant bleeding), not the claimed MACE efficacy outcome; ischemic composite was secondary, higher but NOT significant (HR 1.62, P=0.07, trial underpowered for efficacy) — hence outcome_match=false is honest. population_match correctly true (Korean ACS).
rows.finding: Korean ACS (n=800): clinically significant bleeding significantly higher with ticagrelor (11.7% vs 5.3% clopidogrel, HR 2.26); ischemic composite (CV death/MI/stroke) numerically higher but not significant (9.2% vs 5.8%, HR 1.62, 95% CI 0.96-2.74, P=0.07) — no efficacy benefit and net bleeding harm in this population.

rows.citation: Geravandi M, et al. A comparison of the effects of ticagrelor and clopidogrel in patients with acute STEMI: a systematic review and meta-analysis of RCTs. BMC Pharmacol Toxicol. 2024;25(1):93. DOI:10.1186/s40360-024-00817-8.
rows.integrity_note: 11 RCTs, 5,274 ticagrelor / 5,295 clopidogrel STEMI patients; directionally favors ticagrelor but authors explicitly state effects were NOT statistically significant — supports direction with modest certainty. Re-verified against PubMed abstract.
rows.finding: Pooled STEMI RCTs: ticagrelor associated with lower mortality, recurrent MI, stroke, and MACE vs clopidogrel, with no difference in BARC>=3 major bleeding or TIMI flow — though none of these differences reached statistical significance.

rows.citation: FDA approval of BRILINTA (ticagrelor), 2011, to reduce thrombotic CV events in ACS — regulatory action based on PLATO (Wallentin, NEJM 2009; DOI:10.1056/NEJMoa0904327); reflected in ACC/AHA and ESC ACS guidelines recommending ticagrelor preferentially over clopidogrel.
rows.integrity_note: Regulatory/guideline row anchored to the checkable PLATO pivotal source (PMID:19717846); FDA label carries the CV-event-reduction indication in ACS. Consensus verified as honest.
rows.finding: FDA approved ticagrelor for reduction of thrombotic CV events in ACS on the strength of PLATO; guideline bodies (ACC/AHA, ESC) give ticagrelor a preferred recommendation over clopidogrel in ACS — codifying consensus support for the claim.
